name: Cantonese
variety: Hong Kong Cantonese (close to the Guangzhou standard; differences noted)
sources: Zee, Eric (1999). Chinese (Hong Kong Cantonese). In Handbook of the International Phonetic Association, Cambridge University Press, 58-60.
Bauer, Robert S. & Benedict, Paul K. (1997). Modern Cantonese Phonology. Mouton de Gruyter.
Matthews, Stephen & Yip, Virginia (2011). Cantonese: A Comprehensive Grammar, 2nd edition. Routledge.
Yue-Hashimoto, Anne O. (1972). Phonology of Cantonese. Cambridge University Press.
Chen, Matthew Y. (2000). Tone Sandhi: Patterns across Chinese Dialects. Cambridge University Press.
Yu, Alan C. L. (2007). Understanding near mergers: the case of morphological tone in Cantonese. Phonology 24, 187-214.
Lisker, Leigh & Abramson, Arthur S. (1964). A cross-language study of voicing in initial stops: acoustical measurements. Word 20, 384-422.
Mok, Peggy P. K. (2009). On the syllable-timing of Cantonese and Beijing Mandarin. Chinese Journal of Phonetics 2.
Mok, Peggy P. K., Zuo, Donghui & Wong, Peggy W. Y. (2013). Production and perception of a sound change in progress: tone merging in Hong Kong Cantonese. Language Variation and Change 25.

Wong, Wai Yi P., Chan, Marjorie K. M. & Beckman, Mary E. (2005). An autosegmental-metrical analysis and prosodic annotation conventions for Cantonese. In Sun-Ah Jun (ed.), Prosodic Typology. Oxford University Press.
Ma, Joan K.-Y., Ciocca, Valter & Whitehill, Tara L. (2006). Effect of intonation on Cantonese lexical tones. Journal of the Acoustical Society of America 120.
Yu, Kristine M. & Lam, Hiu Wai (2014). The role of creaky voice in Cantonese tonal perception. Journal of the Acoustical Society of America 136.
Kong, Qing-Ming (1987). Influence of tones upon vowel duration in Cantonese. Language and Speech 30.
contrasts: aspirated versus unaspirated in stops and affricates (p pʰ, t tʰ, k kʰ, kʷ kʷʰ, ts tsʰ); no voiced obstruents
long aː versus short ɐ in closed syllables and diphthongs (saam1 'three' against sam1 'heart', gaai1 'street' against gai1 'chicken')
six tones in open and nasal-final syllables, three in checked syllables
three final nasals m n ŋ and three unreleased final stops p t k
front rounded vowels yː and œː (with its short partner ɵ)
two syllabic nasals, m̩ and ŋ̍
allophony: final p t k have no audible release and are glottally reinforced; place is carried by the formant transitions of the preceding vowel

the short high and mid vowels are positional: [ɪ] and [ʊ] occur only before k and ŋ (Jyutping ik, ing, uk, ung), [ɵ] only before t, n and in the diphthong ɵy (Jyutping eot, eon, eoi), [e] and [o] only in the diphthongs ei and ou
ts tsʰ s are alveolar, moving toward alveolo-palatal before the front rounded vowels yː and œː
initial n is replaced by l by most younger Hong Kong speakers (nei5 'you' said lei5)
initial ŋ is variably dropped, or added to zero-initial syllables; syllabic ŋ̍ is often replaced by m̩ (ng5 'five' said m5)
kʷ and kʷʰ lose their rounding before ɔː for many speakers (gwok3 said gok3)
final ŋ and k are fronted to n and t after some vowels by many younger speakers
zero-initial syllables begin with a glottal stop
the high level tone 55 has a high falling variant 53, contrastive for some older Guangzhou speakers but not in Hong Kong
syllable_structure: (C)V(C) plus tone, or a syllabic nasal plus tone; the coda is one of m n ŋ p t k or an offglide i, u or y
phonotactics: no consonant clusters (kʷ and kʷʰ are single consonants)
codas are limited to m n ŋ p t k and the offglides
checked syllables (ending in p t k) carry only the three level tones: high 5, mid 3, low 2
in checked syllables the high tone goes with short vowels and the mid tone mostly with long vowels
labial initials do not combine with labial codas (dissimilation), apart from a few colloquial words
long vowels are followed by short codas and short vowels by long codas, so rhyme duration is roughly constant

stress.rule: Every syllable carries a full lexical tone and full vowel; there is no neutral tone and no stress placement rule.
stress.cues: prominence for focus is carried by lengthening and expanded pitch range, not by a stress accent

rhythm.notes: More evenly syllable-timed than Beijing Mandarin, since there is no neutral tone or vowel reduction (Mok 2009). Syllable fusion occurs in fast casual speech.

length.notes: Length is contrastive only for the low vowels, aː against ɐ, and is tied to quality. Elsewhere long and short qualities are in complementary distribution. A short vowel is followed by a longer coda, so the rhyme as a whole keeps about the same duration.

intonation.declarative: lexical tones are kept; declination across the utterance and lowering of the last syllable; much of the attitudinal and sentence-type meaning is carried by sentence-final particles, which have their own tones
intonation.yes_no_question: usually marked by a particle (maa3, aa4, me1) or by A-not-A form with no special melody; a question without a particle (echo or declarative question) has a high rising boundary tone on the last syllable, so that every tone ends high and resembles tone 2 (Ma, Ciocca & Whitehill 2006)
intonation.wh_question: statement-like declination; often ends in the particle aa3 or ne1
intonation.continuation: level or slightly raised end of the phrase with lengthening of the last syllable, then pitch reset
intonation.accent_shape: no pitch accents; boundary tones on the final syllable are added to the lexical tone (Wong, Chan & Beckman 2005)
intonation.notes: Because pitch is heavily used for lexical tone, the intonational rise or fall is concentrated on the last syllable or on a particle.

inventory.name: tone 1, high level (陰平 yin ping)
inventory.description: High level. A high falling variant 53 occurs, no longer contrastive in Hong Kong.

inventory.name: tone 1 variant, high falling (older 陰平)
inventory.description: High falling variant of tone 1, kept apart from 55 by some older Guangzhou speakers; eSpeak NG has it as a separate tone phoneme and its dictionary uses it for some characters (三 saam7).

inventory.name: tone 2, high rising (陰上 yin shang)
inventory.description: Rise from low-mid to high, also written 35. It is also the shape of the changed tone.
inventory.connected_speech: 25 or 35; the rise is kept in all positions
inventory.duration: slightly longer than the level tones

inventory.name: tone 3, mid level (陰去 yin qu)
tone 4, low falling (陽平 yang ping)
inventory.description: Low falling to the bottom of the range, also described as extra low level 11.
inventory.phonation: modal, often creaky toward the end; creak helps listeners identify this tone (Yu & Lam 2014)

inventory.name: tone 5, low rising (陽上 yang shang)
inventory.description: Rise from low to mid, also written 13. Merging with tone 2 for some younger speakers.
inventory.duration: slightly longer than the level tones

inventory.name: tone 6, low level (陽去 yang qu)
inventory.description: Low level, about one step below tone 3. Merging with tone 3 for some younger speakers.

inventory.name: high checked tone (上陰入; traditional tone 7, Jyutping 1 before p t k)
inventory.description: High level on a syllable closed by p, t or k, with a short vowel.
inventory.phonation: modal, cut off by the glottalised unreleased stop

inventory.name: mid checked tone (下陰入; traditional tone 8, Jyutping 3 before p t k)
inventory.description: Mid level on a checked syllable, mostly with long vowels.
inventory.phonation: modal, cut off by the glottalised unreleased stop
inventory.duration: short, but longer than the high checked tone because the vowel is long

inventory.name: low checked tone (陽入; traditional tone 9, Jyutping 6 before p t k)
inventory.description: Low level on a checked syllable, with long or short vowels.
inventory.phonation: modal, cut off by the glottalised unreleased stop

sandhi: no productive, phonologically conditioned tone sandhi in present-day Hong Kong Cantonese
older Guangzhou rule: high falling 53 became 55 before another high tone (55, 53 or checked 5); void where 53 and 55 have merged

changed tone (變音 pinjam), lexically and morphologically conditioned: a syllable with a non-high tone (mostly tones 4, 5, 6, also 3), usually the last syllable of a noun or a familiar name, takes a high rising tone like tone 2 (人 jan4 becomes jan2 in 男人, 話 waa6 becomes waa2 in 廣東話, 銀 ngan4 becomes ngan2 'money', 陳 can4 becomes can2 in 老陳); the derived rise is nearly but not fully merged with lexical tone 2 (Yu 2007)
high level changed tone 55 in some words and in kinship reduplication, often with tone 4 on the first syllable (媽媽 maa4 maa1, 爸爸 baa4 baa1, 哥哥 go4 go1; 妹妹 mui4 mui2 has the rising changed tone)
fusion: when 一 jat1 is dropped from a reduplicated form the first syllable takes the rising changed tone (試一試 becomes si2 si3)
intonational boundary tones change the end of the last syllable's tone, most clearly the high rise of particle-less questions
tone.neutral_tone: none; every syllable, including particles, carries a full tone
tone.notes: Tone mergers in progress among younger Hong Kong speakers: tone 2 with tone 5, tone 3 with tone 6, tone 4 with tone 6 (Mok, Zuo & Wong 2013). Tones 3 and 6 lie only about one Chao step apart and are the most confusable pair. Tonal coarticulation is mainly carry-over. Kong (1987) found that vowel duration depends on the tone, with longer vowels under the rising tones. No absolute F0 values are given here.

phonation: creaky voice at the end of the low falling tone 4
glottal reinforcement of the unreleased final stops
no phonation contrast in consonants; aspiration only

problems: the unaspirated stops p t k kʷ are spoken with the voiced stops b d g of the base table, so they are voiced instead of voiceless unaspirated

the affricates differ in place instead of aspiration: unaspirated ts (phoneme z) uses the alveolar affricate recording ustop/ts, which the Mandarin table uses for its aspirated affricate, and aspirated tsʰ (phoneme c) uses the palato-alveolar recording ustop/tsh

no sentence intonation and no declination: CalcPitches_Tone() in src/libespeak-ng/intonation.c has no Cantonese branch and ignores the clause type; a question gives the same audio as a statement, so the rising boundary tone of particle-less questions is missing

the tonal pitch range is very small: the six tones lie between about 76 and 98 Hz at the default voice pitch (about 4.4 semitones, measured on the output); tone 3 (about 86 Hz) and tone 6 (about 81 Hz) are one semitone apart

changed tones exist only where the dictionary lists them (女人 has jan2), and the large list dictsource/extra/yue_listx overrides the small one: 話 is waa2 in yue_list but waa6 in yue_listx, so 廣東話 ends in waa6
syllabic m̩ is missing from the phoneme table; 唔 is listed as ng4 and spoken as a syllabic velar nasal
no shortening of long vowels in checked syllables beyond what the vowel phoneme itself has, and no glottal reinforcement of final stops
no creaky phonation on tone 4; rising tones are not longer than level tones
the voice attribute 'words 1' puts a short pause between words, so speech is staccato; there is no tonal coarticulation
with this voice Latin letters are read as English (dictrules 1), so Jyutping text is not understood; use yue-Latn-jyutping for that
good: the six tones have the right shapes and relative heights (level 50, rise 30 to 50, level 30, fall 20 to 10, rise 10 to 30, level 20 on eSpeak's pitch scale, that is 55, 35, 33, 21, 13, 22)
long and short low vowels differ in both quality and length (aa 230 against a 150 units), and so do the diphthong pairs aai/ai and aau/au
final p t k are silent closures before a pause or another consonant (WAV(NULL)), with formant transitions on the vowel, which matches unreleased stops
the lax allophones of i and u before k and ŋ are implemented
the front rounded vowels yu, oe and eo are present

notes: eSpeak NG applies no tone sandhi to Cantonese: the C code in intonation.c handles only Mandarin, Hakka and one Vietnamese case.
